article_text:
Lobbying groups representing the hotel and travel industries have endorsed a 20% federal tax incentive for film and TV production, arguing that domestic filming attracts tourism from abroad.

The American Hotel & Lodging Association and the U.S. Travel Association have joined an alliance of film industry stakeholders in pushing for the bill. The two groups represent airlines, ticketing sites, hotel companies and resorts, including the Disney and Universal theme parks.

Related Stories

Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden Revenues Climb 11% to $390 Million Thanks to ‘Harry Potter’ Tour, Increased Production (EXCLUSIVE)

‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts James Potter and Lily Potter, Plus Charlie Weasley in Character's Screen Debut

“Every film and TV production made in America sends a ripple through the travel economy, filling hotel rooms, restaurants and small businesses during the shoot and inspiring travelers to visit long after the credits roll,” said Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of the U.S. Travel Association, in a statement. “A federal production incentive would bring that economic activity back to communities in all 50 states and give destinations of every size a powerful new way to showcase themselves to the world.”

A bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act last month. The bill would create a 20% tax credit for labor on film and TV productions in the U.S., with 5% bonuses for independent film and for filming in rural areas and disaster zones.

The bill now has 52 sponsors in the House of Representatives and 10 sponsors in the Senate. The House sponsors are heavily concentrated in filming states, with 15 from California, six from Pennsylvania, four from New York, and three each from New Jersey, Illinois and Georgia.

The House bill has been referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax legislation, while the Senate version is in the Finance Committee. Supporters are hoping to pass the bill during the lame duck session that begins a week after the midterm election.

“The economic benefits of this measure extend well beyond the film and television industry,” said Ralph Posner, spokesman for the American Hotel & Lodging Association. “Domestic production brings cast, crew, and suppliers into communities across the U.S., bolstering hotel demand and supporting local businesses. By encouraging more domestic production activity, the legislation will help drive economic growth, support local communities, and showcase U.S. destinations to audiences around the world.”

Backers of the bill also include the Motion Picture Association, which represents the major studios, as well as the Independent Film and Television Alliance all of the Hollywood unions.

article_text:
Ranbir Kapoor and Yash , stars of the epic adaptation “ Ramayana : Rise of a Legend,” opened Gold House ’s largest Gold Diwali to date at The Majestic Downtown in Los Angeles, alongside filmmakers Nitesh Tiwari and Namit Malhotra, a week before the film’s release.

Gold House, which works to back and celebrate the Asian Pacific community, staged the gathering ahead of Diwali, which falls on Nov. 8 this year. The organization pitched “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” as the biggest film ever produced out of India. Based on the ancient epic, it opens worldwide on Nov. 5, and a DJ set and dance floor themed around the movie ran through the night.

The group also used the evening to unveil the Gold Stack Shorts Fund, a partnership with South Stack Studios that will support proof-of-concept shorts and micro-series built on South Asian stories. Submissions are open through Nov. 30, with the chosen projects to be named Jan. 10, before Sundance.

“Diwali is a celebration of light, community and connection, and we wanted to bring that spirit to our Gold Diwali while honoring how culture shapes who we are and the possibilities we create,” said Bing Chen, Gold House’s executive chair and CEO.

Indian luxury designer Anita Dongre debuted a one-off carrom board, painted by hand in collaboration with Gold House, that recasts the tabletop game common in South Asian homes as a contemporary design object. Guests also saw the Cuyana x Gold House Marigold Charm, a limited-edition piece released earlier in October.

Co-hosts spanned entertainment, media, fashion and business. Among them were Tan France, Freida Pinto, Avantika, Sarayu Blue, Dhar Mann, Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash, Poshmark chairman Manish Chandra and Kabir Ahuja, McKinsey’s global head of TMT and consumer technology. Anita Dongre and Yash Dongre were also among the co-hosts, as was South Stack Studios.

The guest list included Saheli Khan, Aishu Devan and Sehaj Sethi of “Avatar: Seven Havens,” along with Hannah Simone, Janina Gavankar, Manish Dayal, Sanya Malhotra, Richa Moorjani, Nisha Ganatra, Asif Ali, Michelle Khare and Avani Gregg.

Rasoi Catering served regional South Asian dishes, and a lounge was set aside for carrom. DJ MissNinja shared the music with KVS Tabla, an act that fuses tabla with electronic music and other styles. Bhindi Jewelers hosted a jewelry experience, while dating app Dil Mil sponsored a portrait station produced by The Lounge Booth. Smartwater, Glance, McKinsey & Company and Google’s 100 Zeros also backed the event, which was produced by BMF Productions.

In remarks during the night, Chen said Gold Diwali was not just for the Festival of Lights. “It’s for the creators, founders, and true builders who know that shining, that overnight success, is decades in the making,” he said.

The party follows the recent rollout of Gold House’s Diwali Cultural Guide.

article_text:
The celebrated Prince Charles repertory cinema in London’s Leicester Square has announced that the threat of closure has been staved off by signing a new 25-year lease with its landlords.

In a post on social media titled “You Saved the PCC”, the cinema said that “after 21 months of uncertainty, we’re delighted to have secured the future of the cinema” and that they had “signed a new 25-year lease with no break clause, ensuring our projectors will keep rolling for years to come”.

The cinema also expressed its gratitude for the “support, commitment and belief of many, many people”.

In January 2025, the Prince Charles launched a petition , claiming that its landlord, Zedwell LSQ Ltd (owned by developer Criterion Capital) was trying to “bully us out of the building” by demanding a break clause in its lease, due for renewal in September 2025. The break clause would have enabled Zedwell to give the cinema six months’ notice if it had other plans for the site. At the time, Criterion Capital denied that it was attempting to intimidate or disadvantage the cinema.

The news, however, triggered a groundswell of support, from film fans and industry figures including the actor Paul Mescal and directors Danny Boyle, Robert Eggers, Christopher Nolan and Edgar Wright .

The building was opened as a live theatre in 1962 , but converted to a cinema in 1969 after being bought by the Star Cinema chain, and subsequently showed adult movies. In 1991 it was taken over as a repertory cinema with cut-price seats. In May 2025, the Prince Charles was designated an asset of community value by Westminster City Council.

Ben Freedman, the owner of the Prince Charles, said in a statement: “Our cinema means an enormous amount to our team, our audiences and the wider arts community. Having this security gives us the confidence to invest in the cinema’s future and continue providing a home for film lovers. We are pleased to have reached an agreement that works for both parties and, most importantly, allows us to look forward with real confidence and excitement to the next chapter of the Prince Charles Cinema.”

Vaqas Farooq, CEO of Criterion Capital, said: “We are delighted to have agreed terms which secure [the Prince Charles’] future … I’m particularly pleased that together we were able to work through a set of complex issues and find an equitable solution for both parties. A 25-year commitment provides real security for the cinema and its fans, and we are delighted to be continuing our partnership for many years to come.” Farooq added that the landlords plan to develop a hotel on the building’s upper floors.

Lease issues are also behind the threat to another key independent cinema , the Ultimate Picture Palace in Oxford, whose landlord, the University of Oxford’s Oriel College, is refusing to renew its current lease past 2037.

Daily Newsletter

Vermeer the Immortal

Tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring influence, free back-to-school art supplies for NYC teachers, and a glitch at a Pioneer Works exhibition is unexpectedly illuminating.

Vermeer is everywhere. Not only in the hallowed halls of museums, but also in the gentle light that streams through the window just so, or in the crisp pages of a love letter set down gently at one’s writing desk. Historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell seems to agree in Vermeer’s Afterlives , her new title tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring presence across the arts, from film to verse. Lauren Moya Ford brings us into its exquisitely illustrated pages.

In another must-read today, a glitch at Finnegan Shannon’s Pioneer Works exhibition yields insights on institutions and accessibility. “The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world,” Bryan Martin writes, “a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it.”Hyperallergic Halloween is around the corner. RSVP for our art costume party with snacks and an open bar in Brooklyn on Wednesday, October 28 — members get discounted tickets!

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places

As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. | Lauren Moya Ford

article_text:
Walking into Tate Modern ‘s Turbine Hall on Monday morning, I experienced an initial wave of disappointment. The latest commission for the space, by Tarek Atoui , is certainly no spectacle. The hovering assemblage of bamboo frames, instruments, and draped electrical wires—all in a subtle color scheme of gray, beige, and orange—looks a bit like a cross between a boiler room and a mid-tier design store.

However, if the installation, Hold , lacks the immediate wow factor of some of its predecessors, it proffers instead a new way of experiencing the cavernous, post-industrial space.

The environment is filled with instruments, including Korean drums, Uzbek horns, gongs, and shengs, strung up beside glowing, amber-toned lights. Large slabs of stone litter the ground, providing spots for visitors to sit. D.J. equipment covers one long, altar-like surface toward the back of the room.

Installation view of Tarek Atoui’s commission at Tate Modern, 2026. Photo: Susan Davis.

The surrounding space reverberated with sound on my visit: at one time with a deep, bellowing thrum, and later with a more melodic tinkle. At one point, the proud, yawning call of a horn unfurled at its leisure. It is a sound you can imagine commanding attention at any time in human history. The music is ever-changing, generated by a complex computer program crafted by Atoui.

The Lebanese artist, who lives in Paris, sees the installation as a culmination of two decades of musical collaborations. “Each instrument has a history, has a story,” he said at a press preview for the show.

But it is also a starting point of sorts. He has asked several musicians to respond to the space in a series of live sessions , which kick off this week with Mazen Kerbaj , Kenichi Iwasa , and Aya Metwalli . There will also be a program of workshops.

“It’s not an easy space to tame,” Atoui said, explaining that he picked performers he believes will be sensitive to its quirks. Sufficiently curious practitioners will be able to “play the whole space like an instrument,” he said.

Installation view of Tarek Atoui’s commission at Tate Modern, 2026. Photo: Susan Davis.

The Turbine Hall is a commission that many in the art world love to hate. In the wake of so many failed wannabe showstoppers, including last year’s much-criticized tribute to Sámi ancestral knowledge, the vast space might strike a new artist as overpowering, rather than inviting. I always hope to encounter something able to fill the venue and redefine it.

Atoui achieves this, but not in a way we’ve seen before. He conjures sculpture out of sound and, still more intangibly, asks us to gather, mingle, and improvise our own sounds in response. If this vision comes together as he describes it, his creation may prove surprisingly memorable.

“Tarek Atoui: Hold” is on view through April 11, 2027 in the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern.

Kveum）讲述了15岁的克里斯（Chris）的故事，她被朋友玛雅（Maja）说服，一同参加一个夏令营。在那里聚集着致力于拯救瑞典森林的青少年。除了营火聚会和湖畔远足外，还组织了针对砍伐树木的破坏活动。直到人们发现营地领袖埃利亚斯（Elias）的生态承诺背后隐藏着仇外野心。在营地的一些男孩挑起与一名年轻难民的斗殴之后，发生了一起针对寻求庇护者收容所的夜间袭击。克里斯参与其中，拍摄了行动并发布了一段仇外短片。这导致她与失望离开的玛雅决裂。", "Filmdienst", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "凭借充满暗示性的画面序列，《Nipster》成功揭示了极右翼分子的狡猾陷阱，他们以所谓的理想主义将幼稚的青少年拉入自己的势力范围。从无害的集会开始，经由产生深远影响的干扰行动和封锁，最终走向激进化和暴力。主演萨加·斯滕曼非常可信地展现了这一灾难性的发展，但导演手法有时采用了过于直白的手段。摄像机经常表现出过度雄心勃勃的晃动，即使事件本身并不需要如此，而那些来自社交媒体、夹杂着仇恨信息的狂热短片大多显得过于煽情。《Nipster》的一个巨大优点反而是它的结尾，它悬置了克里斯是成功摆脱意识形态激进化还是深陷右翼势力范围的结局。正是通过这一点，该电影为反思青少年中一种危险的社会趋势提供了良好的启发。", article_text:
Beim Schlingel-Filmfestival in Chemnitz wird das Kino für die ganze Familie großgeschrieben, was explizit auch die jüngsten Besucher im Vorschulalter einschließt. Eine eigene Reihe widmete sich Filmen für Kinder unter sechs Jahren. Mehr als 25.000 Besucher freuten sich an bewegenden Geschichten und außergewöhnlichen Abenteuern. Unter den Jugendfilmen sorgte der schwedische Film „Nipster“ über ein Sommerlager von Rechtsextremen für viele Diskussionen.

Wie führt man kleine Kinder ans Kino heran? Am besten, indem man ihnen altersgerechte Filme zeigt. Doch das ist gar nicht so einfach. Denn viele Menschen, die Kinderkinos betreiben, klagen schon lange, dass zu wenige Filme für die jüngste Zielgruppe hergestellt werden. Beim 31. Schlingel-Filmfestival für Kinder und junges Publikum (2.-10.10.2026) in Chemnitz gab es endlich auch eine Reihe von Filmen zu sehen, die für Kinobesucher ab fünf oder sechs Jahren gedacht sind.

Als Publikumsrenner erwies sich dabei der deutsche Puppenspielfilm „ Der Regenbogenfisch “. Der fünfte lange Kinofilm der legendären Augsburger Puppenkiste beruht auf der gleichnamigen Buchreihe von Marcus Pfister. Regisseur Florian Moch und das Marionettenspielteam erzählen vom eitlen Regenbogenfisch, der besonders stolz auf seine glänzenden Schuppen ist. Statt mit den anderen Meeresbewohnern zu spielen, putzt er ständig seine Schuppen und manövriert sich darüber in die Einsamkeit. Als er eines Tages eine Schuppe verliert, muss er in die Tiefsee tauchen, um sie wiederzufinden. Nur widerwillig lässt er sich vom kleinen blauen Fisch begleiten. Auf ihrer gemeinsamen Suche erleben die beiden eine Reihe von Abenteuern und begegnen seltsamen Wesen wie dem aufschneiderischen Fisch Humbrecht oder dem Grummel-Grusel-Fisch.

Für die deutsch-schweizerische Co-Produktion wurden prominente Schauspieler wie Jannik Schümann, Luna Wedler, Bjarne Mädel, Oliver Kalkofe oder Andrea Sawatzki gewonnen, die den Bewohnern der Unterwasserwelt ihre Stimmen leihen. Die schrulligen Charaktere, die Kulissen des kunterbunten Riffs, die beschwingten Musical-Einlagen und das stetige Wasserplätschern und -gluckern lassen die Fäden der handgeführten Marionetten schnell vergessen. Mit nur 67 Minuten Spielzeit kommen die kleinkindgerechten Episoden zudem der Aufmerksamkeitsspanne der kleinsten Kinogänger entgegen.

Einen prall gefüllten Kinosaal gab es auch bei der Aufführung von „ Das NEINhorn – Der Film “. Der amüsante Animationsfilm beruht auf dem gleichnamigen Buch von Marc-Uwe Kling und Astrid Henn. Im Zentrum steht ein notorischer Neinsager. Obwohl das kleine Einhorn in einer glücklichen Familie aufwächst, sagt es zu allem „Nein!“ Deshalb wird das Tier mit dem kleinen Horn von den Bewohnern des Herzwaldes, die stets in Reimen sprechen, nur noch „NEINhorn“ genannt. Eines Tages dreht es der rosaroten Idylle den Rücken zu und wandert nach NIRGENDS, wo es endlich alles tun kann, was zu Hause unerwünscht ist, etwa per Arschbombe in ein Schlammloch hüpfen. Unterwegs lernt es den schwerhörigen WASbär und den stoischen NAhUND kennen, der immer wieder „Na und“ sagt. Gemeinsam erleben sie allerlei Abenteuer, bis sie auf eine vorlaute Prinzessin treffen.

Selten hat man in einem Film so gelacht. Marc-Uwe Kling hat den wunderbar schrägen Figuren nicht nur pointierte Dialoge in den Mund gelegt, sondern auch viele Slapstick-Nummern ersonnen, die er zusammen mit Johannes Weiland auch gekonnt inszeniert. Ihr filmisches Loblied auf Quertreiber und Nonkonformisten wirkt nicht zuletzt deshalb so hintersinnig, weil der notorische Verweigerer dem Erzähler der Geschichte so lange widerspricht, bis der kapituliert.

Kindliche Heldenreise im Dschungel

Ein weiteres Animationsabenteuer für Kinder ab sechs Jahren präsentierte der lettische Regisseur Edmunds Jansons mit „ Der magische Dschungel “. Das Drehbuch beruht lose auf den Berichten des lettischen Entdeckers Aleksandars Laime, der von 1942 bis 1994 als Einsiedler in der venezolanischen Wildnis gelebt und unter anderem den höchsten Wasserfall der Welt aufgespürt hat. Im Zentrum des Films steht die neunjährige Elisabeth, die in der Hauptstadt Caracas zur Schule geht, während der Sommerferien aber auf die Orchideeninsel im Dschungel zurückkehrt, wo ihre Eltern und ihr kleiner Bruder Leo leben. Als ihre Eltern zu einem Arztbesuch in die Stadt müssen, soll sie auf Leo aufpassen. Als der beim Spielen spurlos verschwindet, irrt sie auf der Suche nach ihm durch den Dschungel und muss neben ihrem Bruder auch ein magisches Fellwesen retten, das von Wilderern gefangen wurde.

Der Film besticht durch eine spannende, leicht verständliche Geschichte, viele fantastische Figuren, farbenfrohe Zeichnungen und eine abwechslungsreiche Musik. Die elegante Kombination von Legetrick- und Computeranimation kreiert eine heitere Atmosphäre, die immer anzeigt, dass bei allen Abenteuern und Gefahren am Ende alles gut ausgehen wird. Schön anzusehen ist vor allem, wie das Mädchen lernt, Verantwortung zu übernehmen, ohne dass der Film den pädagogischen Zeigefinger bemüht.

Noch viel seltener als Animationsfilme für Vorschulkinder sind Live-Action-Filme für die jüngste Zielgruppe. Wie schwierig sich solche Produktionen realisieren lassen, zeigt das Beispiel des erfahrenen Kinderfilmspezialisten Bernd Sahling, der rund zehn Jahre brauchte, um sein Herzensprojekt „ Koschka “ umsetzen zu können. Und das, obwohl es sich dabei sogar um einen Katzenfilm handelt. In dem 75-minütigen Werk läuft dem achtjährigen Jan eine getigerte Katze zu, die er „Koschka“ nennt, weil sie auf diesen Namen zu reagieren scheint. Als Koschka im Schrank drei Junge zur Welt bringt, kümmert sich Jan mit seinem Freund Sami und der Mitschülerin Martha um die Tiere. Jan verzichtet sogar auf eine Urlaubsreise mit seiner Mutter, die getrennt von seinem Vater lebt. Bis eine Ärztin eine Allergie gegen Katzenhaare bei Jan diagnostiziert. Die Katze und ihre Jungen können nicht länger in der Wohnung bleiben. Landen sie nun im Tierheim?

Man merkt der Inszenierung an, dass Sahling Katzen liebt, obwohl der Regisseur selbst von einer leichten Allergie gegen ihre Haare geplagt wird. Die Geschichte ist recht überschaubar, aber altersgerecht mit liebevoller Hand in Szene gesetzt. Im Subtext des charmanten Plots um die Freundschaft zwischen Tier und Mensch hat Sahling zudem eine humanitäre Botschaft untergebracht. Denn Jan spricht auch Russisch; seine Mutter ist mit ihm aus Russland eingewandert. Insofern teilen Koschka und Jan in gewisser Weise das gleiche Schicksal, nämlich Geflüchtete zu sein .

Ein Animationsjuwel: „Iron Boy“

Sehenswerte Filme konnte man beim „Schlingel“-Festival aber nicht nur in der Kinderfilm-Sektion entdecken. Das größte deutsche Kinder- und Jugendfilmfestival präsentierte auch in den Sektionen „Juniorfilm“ (elf bis 13 Jahre) und „Jugendfilm“ (ab 14 Jahre) überzeugende Filme. Die meisten Auszeichnungen sammelte dabei der Zeichentrickfilm „ Iron Boy “ von Louis Clichy ein. Der Film erzählt von dem elfjährigen Franzosen Christophe, der ein Korsett aus Metall tragen muss, weil er ohne dieses Hilfsmittel schlicht umkippen würde. Wegen seiner körperlichen Einschränkung ist er auf dem Bauernhof seiner Eltern keine große Hilfe. Sein starrköpfiger Vater nimmt ihn nicht ernst und stützt sich lieber auf Christophes größeren Bruder. Auch in der Schule wird Christophe zum Außenseiter.

Lebensfreude entdeckt er erst wieder, als der Organist in der Kirche sein musikalisches Talent entdeckt und ihn fördert. Dann lernt er beim rückenstärkenden Schwimmen auch noch Clara kennen, die ein Jahr älter, aber sehr viel selbstbewusster als er ist. Als der Bauernhof in eine finanzielle Schieflage gerät, spitzt sich die Situation zu. Soll Christophe ein wichtiges Konzert sausen lassen, um bei der Ernte zu helfen?

„Iron Boy“ ist der erste eigene Film von Louis Clichy, der als Animator bei Pixar-Filmen wie „Ratatouille“, „WALL-E“ und „Oben“ gearbeitet und bei zwei französischen „Asterix“-Filmen als Co-Regisseur beteiligt war. In der bewegenden Selbstermächtigungserzählung hat der Filmemacher eigene Erfahrungen verarbeitet. Er wuchs selbst auf einem Bauernhof auf und musste ein Stützkorsett tragen. Auf faszinierende Weise gelingt es „Iron Boy“, in feinfühligen Bildfolgen daran teilhaben zu lassen, wie ein junger Außenseiter Widerstände überwindet und Freundschaft, Selbstvertrauen und schließlich seinen eigenen Weg ins Leben findet. Die handwerkliche Qualität der Animation ist herausragend; hier genügen beschwingte Linien und sanfte Aquarellfarben, um eine komplexe Welt zu erschaffen. Eine große Stärke liegt auch in der vielschichtigen Orgelmusik, die zusammen mit einem Sounddesign eine pralle Klangwelt entstehen lässt. Zudem versteht es der Film meisterhaft, ernste Themen wie Behinderung und Finanznot mit Poesie, Romantik, Zärtlichkeit, Fantasie und einer Prise Humor zu verbinden.

In der Außenseiterposition

Unter den Jugendfilmen stachen vor allem zwei Produktionen hervor: „ I Matter “ und „ Congo Boy “. In „I Matter“ erzählt die rumänische Regisseurin Alina Șerban von einer 17-jährigen Romni, die in einem Waisenhaus aufwächst; sie muss das Heim allerdings demnächst verlassen, wenn sie 18 Jahre alt wird. Als junge Frau schafft sie den Sprung an eine Schauspielschule, sieht sich aber weiterhin mit Ausgrenzung, Armut, Einsamkeit und Diskriminierung konfrontiert. Spannungsreich ist auch die Beziehung zu ihrem fremden Vater, als der endlich aus dem Gefängnis entlassen wird. Doch die Wiederannäherung fällt schwerer als erwartet.

Die kraftvolle Inszenierung wird vor allem von der ausdrucksstarken Romani-Schauspielerin Denisa Farcaș getragen. „ I Matter “ ist ein mitreißender Film über die Sehnsucht nach Geborgenheit, Mut, Beharrlichkeit und weibliche Selbstbestimmung; in Chemnitz wurde er mit dem Preis der Ökumenischen Jury ausgezeichnet. In der Begründung lobt die Jury: „Der Film gibt den Erfahrungen jener jungen Menschen einen künstlerischen Raum, deren Stimmen sonst im Getöse von Rassismus, Klassismus und Adultismus leise zu werden droht.“

In einer Außenseiterposition befindet sich auch der Protagonist in dem Familiendrama „ Congo Boy “. Darin geht es um den 17-jährigen Kongolesen Robert. Er träumt davon, in Bangui, der Hauptstadt der Demokratischen Republik Kongo, mit seiner Hip-Hop-Musik genug Geld zu verdienen, um sich und seine vier jüngeren Geschwister durchzubringen; seine Eltern sitzen wegen Passvergehen im Gefängnis. Robert versucht überdies, einen Schulabschluss zu schaffen, gerät aber in die Wirren des Bürgerkrieges.

Auch „Congo Boy“ ist autobiografisch geprägt. Regisseur Rafiki Fariala, ein Multitalent, das eigene Rap-Songs in den Film einbringt, wurde 1997 in der DR Kongo geboren. Auf der Flucht vor dem Bürgerkrieg landete er mit seinen Eltern in Bangui, wo er später Wirtschaftswissenschaften studierte. Die energiegeladene Inszenierung gewährt einen aufschlussreichen Blick in eine wenig bekannte Lebenswelt und besticht mit einer abwechslungsreichen Musik und dem ausdrucksstarken Hauptdarsteller Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset, der sich zu einer kraftvollen Identifikationsfigur entwickelt. Die Figuren und ihre Erlebnisse sind schlüssig in die Milieus eingebettet, wobei auch die innerafrikanische Diskriminierung von Geflüchteten thematisiert wird.

Fallstricke der Rechten

Der am meisten diskutierte Film war der Jugendfilm „ Nipster “ aus Schweden. Das Kunstwort „ Nipster “ setzt sich aus „Nazi“ und „Hipster“ zusammen und bezeichnet einen rechtsextremistischen Menschen, der sich äußerlich und lebensweltlich an der urbanen Hipster-Subkultur orientiert. Die Regisseurin Sunniva Eir Tangvik Kveum erzählt von der 15-jährigen Chris, die sich von ihrer Freundin Maja überreden lässt, gemeinsam an einem Sommercamp teilzunehmen. Dort treffen sich Jugendliche, die sich für die Rettung der schwedischen Wälder einsetzen. Neben Zusammenkünften am Lagerfeuer und Ausflügen zum Badesee werden auch Sabotageaktionen gegen die Abholzung der Bäume organisiert. Bis sich herausstellt, dass der Lagerleiter Elias hinter dem Öko-Engagement fremdenfeindliche Ambitionen verfolgt. Nachdem einige Jungs aus dem Lager eine Prügelei mit einem jungen Geflüchteten provoziert haben, kommt es zu einem nächtlichen Überfall auf ein Asylbewerberheim. Chris macht mit, filmt die Aktion und postet einen ausländerfeindlichen Clip. Das führt zum Zerwürfnis mit Maja, die enttäuscht abreist.

Mit suggestiven Bildfolgen gelingt es „Nipster“, die raffinierten Fallstricke der Rechtsextremisten deutlich zu machen, die mit einem vermeintlichen Idealismus naive Jugendliche in ihren Dunstkreis locken. Was mit harmlosen Kundgebungen beginnt, führt über folgenreiche Störaktionen und Blockaden zur Radikalisierung und Gewalt. Die Hauptdarstellerin Saga Stenman veranschaulicht sehr glaubhaft diese verhängnisvolle Entwicklung, doch die Inszenierung greift mitunter zu allzu plakativen Mitteln. Die Kamera wackelt oft überambitioniert herum, auch wenn die Ereignisse das nicht erfordern, und die hektischen Clips aus den Sozialen Medien wirken mit ihren Hass-Nachrichten meist zu reißerisch. Ein großer Pluspunkt von „Nipster“ ist hingegen der Schluss, der offenlässt, ob Chris den Ausstieg aus der ideologischen Radikalisierung schafft oder im Dunstkreis der Rechten hängenbleibt. Gerade damit vermittelt der Film gute Anstöße zum Nachdenken über einen gefährlichen gesellschaftlichen Trend unter Teenagern.

article_text:
When the name Baba Yaga is first thrown out in Kat Sandler’s series, “Yaga,” the reaction is what you’d expect from any thirty-something guy in the year 2026: “Wait, the one from ‘John Wick’ ?” The response doubles as an acknowledgement of and explanation for a title that, on its own, sounds weirdly incomplete: “Oh, OK: They couldn’t call it ‘Baba Yaga’ because then everyone would think it’s a ‘John Wick’ show. So it’s just called, ‘Yaga.’ Because it’s actually about witches.”

But “Yaga” is also weirdly incomplete in execution, mainly because it’s not nearly weird enough. Adapted from Sandler’s play of the same name, the eight-episode series reimagines the Baba Yaga myth as a detective-driven mystery — not the myth about Keanu Reeves’ unkillable assassin, but the historical one from Slavic folklore about a witch who, depending on the teller, is either a nice, accommodating, elderly woman, or a kidnapping, kid-eating monster.

Sandler’s story savors teasing both potential interpretations, presenting its witchy characters as simultaneously suspicious and helpful to make sure either explanation remains plausible as long as possible: They’re there to prey on the townsfolk, or they’re there to help our investigators crack the case. Or, perhaps, it’s a little bit of both.

But “Yaga” never reaches its potential as a horror show or a mystery (and I can’t say whether its feminist underpinnings pay off either, since only seven of the eight episodes were made available for review). It’s not scary enough to qualify as the former or be witch ing enough to sustain the latter. Instead, it leans on traditional, less exciting crime drama tropes while stretching out a whodunit that spends way too long pretending the answer won’t involve double, double toil and trouble, burning fire and cauldron bubbles. As fun as it is to watch Carrie-Anne Moss toy with various fuckboys, it would be nice to know why she’s doing it much, much sooner (if at all).

Things pop off with the disappearance of Henry Park (played by “Heated Rivalry’s” Hudson Williams in yet another Crave production ). Henry is the heir to his family fishing empire, but he’s better known around their small, coastal town as a bro who throws great parties. He lives in a giant mansion with one (1) roommate: a friend named Logan who, despite being unrelated, looks exactly like Henry. Both roles are played by Williams, and while neither takes up that much screentime, the actor does a fine job distinguishing the entitled playboy from his quiet, fawning sidekick.

Our leads, of course, are our detectives: There’s Carson (Clark Backo), a by-the-book beat cop in the Whittock police department whose personal life is vastly underdeveloped, and Rapp (Noah Reid), a private investigator flown in (literally) by the Park family who sucks up too much oxygen. When Rapp gets dropped off at Henry’s house by helicopter , Carson takes one look at his outfit and laughs: black skinny tie, black leather jacket, brown leather duffel bag. He’s not dressed for the rainy Canadian countryside, but another cop says exactly what Rapp hopes he’ll say: “I think he looks pretty cool.”

Rapp’s first impression proves right on the nose: He’s impossibly full of himself. Cocksure and brazen, Rapp is paired with Carson by the local chief, but he doesn’t work well with others. He chases his own theories while searching for Henry (which conveniently involve a lot of drug-fueled parties and women amenable to his charms) and follows up however he feels like it (or if he feels like it, in case he’s moved on to another amenable woman). If that means a little unlawful search and seizure, so be it. If it means sleeping with a suspect (or two, or three), well that’s just a perk of the job.

Rapp comes off as such a clichéd bad boy you can’t wait for Carson to pop his inflated ego, and “Yaga” acknowledges that desire almost as quickly as it establishes the need for it. When Rapp climbs out of the helicopter to introduce himself, smoothing his hair back into place after the whirling blades displace his slick, faux-casual styling, he slips and eats dirt. Great! Get him, “Yaga!” This guy sucks, and he could only be coded as more of a douchebag if he was hocking crypto on the side and smoking cigarettes for the health benefits .

But then…he just… sticks around? Unchecked and encouraged for reasons yet unknown? Rapp’s schtick goes on for so long, working his “magic” on so many Whittock women, I found myself wondering, “Is Noah Reid Canada’s version of Ryan Gosling?” No, of course not! Ryan Gosling is Canada’s version of Ryan Gosling! Plus, if anyone in the “Yaga” cast should be treated like the most irresistible man in the northernmost part of North America, it’s Hudson Williams. After “Heated Rivalry,” no one would think twice about that guy going to bed with anyone he wants, even if he also had the worst game in town.

“Yaga” does offer some delicious comeuppance in the form of seductive, empowered suspects like Katherine (Carrie-Anne Moss), a professor who loves bones so much she wrote a book called — I am not kidding — ”Sexy Bones.” And there are a few sexy scenes here and there, although they’re usually creep-ified by ominous narration from a yet-unseen witch, disturbing hallucinations, or Rapp’s involvement.

“Yaga” feels like it’s building to a welcome point — about society’s centuries-long persecution and distrust of women, about the appropriate response to condoned oppression, about bad men with good hair — but the subtext isn’t enough to sustain eight episodes, even when they clock in at roughly 30 minutes apiece. It doesn’t help that our de facto protagonist, Carson, is a complete blank. If she was able or willing to balance out Rapp’s toxic energy, maybe “Yaga” could cast a convincing spell. As is, it’s a lot of incantations without the ensuing enchantment.

Grade: C

“Yaga” premieres Friday, October 23 on AMC+ with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the two-episode finale on Friday, November 27.

article_text:
Archives – October 21, 2015

Here is the second part “ I remember ” by Bernard Plossu , since the early 1970s, he has photographed his friends photographers. His rare portraits were never shown, regularly The Eye of Photography will be presenting a selection.

My portraits are always moments of encounter rather than planned portraits … and so I like to call them encounters.

As a teenager, in the age of the Cinemathèque in the early 60s, I photographed my buddies with my Kodak Retinette. Then came the photos of friends and the shots from my Mexican journey, and in 1966 the road trip to Big Sur: I didn’t know yet that I was really going to become a … photographer!

I’ve met tons of people, and there are some encounters I didn’t photograph, like with my friend Sergio Leone, or Moustaki on his motor bike, or Max Evans the Western writer, or even Gerard Blain in 1963 on Porquerolles! It is all in the moment, I didn’t think … but felt?

An encounter can take place without being photographed…

Sometimes, it’s a request, like in the case of Isidore Isou with Pierre Brochet and C. Schlatter, or an encounter of my dreams, like going to see Albert Cossery at the Hôtel La Louisiane…

But the main thing is, the friendship of the moment, not the scoop, or whatever!

You see, these encounters, they’re a great way of celebrating life! Because there are some incredible moments! Lisette Model so demure, inviting me, “yes Darling,” that’s rare! or Alvarez Bravo poised so simply on a street corner in London!

There are also people one loves and whom one sees often, several portraits over the years, like Denis Roche, Lewis Baltz, Max Pam, Luis Baylon, a life shared.

In a word, these are in fact sentimental encounters! These are photos taken out of a need to take them.

So they are all about the time, the era. Without intending to, they speak of the passing years…

Now, there are portraits of friends who have passed away, and that’s hard… Looking at them demands strength because one misses their voices, their gaze… Of the 5 friends who came with me to the Chiapas jungle in 1966 only one remains! Hampton, an American. These were encounters with people with whom sharing life was magical, whether they were trekkers, travel companions, or writers, artists, or photographers.

So here are a few photographs, from all countries, of all ages and styles, and I’m happy to be able to share these images of all of them with you. Bernard Plossu’s archives are managed by Signatures. http://www.signatures-photographies.com

article_text:
Jesse Eisenberg has said he was frozen out of studio movies after winning a Razzie for Zack Snyder’s “ Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice .”

The Razzies — short for Golden Raspberry Awards — are a tongue-in-cheek ceremony that “honor” the supposedly worst films of the year. They are traditionally handed out the night before the Oscars.

Eisenberg, who played arch villain Lex Luther opposite Henry Cavill and Ben Affleck, was allocated a worst supporting actor Razzie for his part in the 2016 superhero flick.

Related Stories

Mia Goth Slams Instagram’s ‘Incomprehensible’ Decision to Let AI-Altered Selfie Spread Online

Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year

Although supposedly lighthearted, the “award” damaged his acting career, Eisenberg admitted during a screen talk Sunday as part of the BFI London Film Festival , causing him to step back from acting and instead lean in to writing and directing. (Eisenberg’s latest directorial effort, “The Debut” starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, is closing LFF Sunday night).

Popular on Variety

“Listen, a lot of it just came from fear,” he said of his career pivot. “I couldn’t get into movie studio parts anymore because I had won a Raspberry Award from [being in the] ‘Batman’ movie … and I saw the trajectory.”

“If you’re an actor, you’re constantly panicked about ‘Am I on an upslope or a downslope?’” he explained. “Because there’s no plateau. Acting is just this unstable, awful industry where you are either on the treadmill and you’re doing okay and you’re running up or you are yesterday’s news and it’s awful. And if you’re a paranoid person like me, you see it way in advance.”

“So I was like, I’ve got to direct movies. That’s why I started writing them, just to kind of keep my career afloat, really.”

“Batman v Superman,” which opened globally with an impressive $424.1 million box office, took home four Razzies overall, including for worst screenplay, worst sequel and worst screen combo for Cavill and Affleck. Eisenberg has previously said the film’s “poor” reception damaged his career.

At the BFI talk, the actor said his takeaway from the experience was that he shouldn’t star in any more superhero films. “The industry tells you what they want from you,” Eisenberg said. “The industry did not want me to be in a superhero movie, and if you’re smart and self-aware, you learn that quickly. And you know, it’s the unsuccessful actor that goes ‘No, I want to be in more of those.’ It’s not going to happen and they don’t want you there and they wouldn’t have given you a Raspberry Award if they wanted you there. That’s an award for bad acting. And so the industry tells you what it wants and if you want a career in the arts you have to follow the things that you’re being told are liked.”

One role the industry did want to see him reprise was that of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, given Eisenberg was nominated for a best actor Oscar for playing the tech titan in 2010’s “The Social Network,” penned by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher.

Despite that, the actor has been adamant he did not want to return in the recently-released follow-up “The Social Reckoning,” which Sorkin both wrote and directed. He didn’t expand on that decision during his LFF talk, other than to say the “companion movie,” as it has been dubbed, “is quite different.”

He was more open about working with Kieran Culkin in Eisenberg’s sophomore directorial effort “A Real Pain,” which was released in 2024. The movie scored Eisenberg a nod for best screenplay and Culkin a best supporting actor win at last year’s Oscars, but the film could have turned out very differently.

“We didn’t know if Kieran was ever going to show up to Poland,” Eisenberg revealed. “Emma Stone is producing the movie. She personally took him on the plane to Poland [where it was shooting] because we didn’t know if he was going to show up. She sent me a video of him going through customs, saying ‘We are here!’ and then he still was late.”

And Culkin, who’d recently come off HBO’s mega-hit “Succession,” was adamant he wanted Eisenberg to use a similar “spontaneous” shooting style, which had not been part of the plan. “We’re like, what’s best for the movie?” the actor/director recalled as he tried to work out what to do. “And I guess what’s best for the movie is probably following this live wire around because that’s the engine of the movie anyway. If he had a small part, you’d be like, ‘We just have to tell this guy to shut up,’ you know? But he’s the lead… So it was a real learning curve.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: 10月16日，这部Hulu热门犯罪剧集的主演兼执行制片人携手昆西·泰勒·伯恩斯坦、史蒂夫·韦以及作曲家阿里尔·马克斯亮相Vidiots，出席了IndieWire举办的展映及问答活动。

"https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/shows/furious-review-emmy-rossum-hulu-series-1235206884/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/emmy-rossum/"}, {"text": "Vidiots", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/vidiots/"}, {"text": "IndieWire and Disney’s “Pass the Remote” screening of Episode 1 and a conversation", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/events/indiewire-disney-furious-screening-vidiots-1235219327/"}, {"text": "Furious", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/furious/"}], "大堂里装点着万圣节的装饰，全情投入的观众们在随后的招待会上意犹未尽地继续着交流。当晚庆祝的是一部前沿惊悚片，它在一些极其黑暗的角落里找到了人际连接。韦抢尽了风头，就像他在备受瞩目的犯罪剧集中所做的那样——尽管在他的角色阿尔登并没有在我们展映的那一集中出现。这位演员开玩笑说，阿尔登与执法部门的遭遇为这个角色增添了个人色彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screen-Shot-2026-09-30-at-11.34.08-AM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "《Furious》", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Adults-Season-2-cast.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "FX剧集《Adults》第2季演员阵容包括饰演安东的欧文·蒂尔、饰演比利·露西·弗赖尔、饰演保罗·贝克的杰克·伊纳嫩以及饰演伊萨的阿米塔·拉奥", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“如果是我处在那种情况下，”他回忆起当时的心理活动，“我会怎么……去整联邦调查局？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他的答案随后在《Furious》中揭晓，但该剧犀利的喜剧时机在Vidiots得到了充分展现。将这群特殊的问题制造者聚在一起，始于罗森几个夏天前启动的一个复古观看项目。这位明星兼执行制片人表示，4年前她一直在寻找老电影，希望能从中发掘出适合改编成长篇剧集的创意。", "links": [{"text": "Vidiots", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/2026-programmers-jam-repertory-cinema-conference-1235193253/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_A0907.jpg?w=650", "alt": "", "caption": "阿里尔·马克斯、昆西·泰勒·伯恩斯坦、埃米·罗森和史蒂夫·韦在Vidiots出席IndieWire的Pass the Remote座谈会，摄于10月16日（Rich Polk 摄）", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这次搜寻将她引向了鲍勃·雷费尔森执导的《黑寡妇》（Black Widow），这部1987年的惊悚片由黛博拉·温格和特蕾莎·拉塞尔主演。她深深着迷于其剧情的演变：从联邦调查局特工追捕女性连环杀手，转变为两个截然不同的女性之间一段异常动人的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我简直是把创作该剧的想法植入了她的脑海，”罗森在谈到创作者伊丽莎白·梅丽韦瑟时开玩笑说，同时不忘将这位编剧称作真正的《Furious》幕后主脑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗森将这个项目带给了Searchlight和Hulu，此前他们曾与梅丽韦瑟合作过《辍学生》。随后，当被问及是否喜欢这位编剧的作品时，罗森不假思索地回答：“对我来说，这绝对是稳操胜券的‘yes’。”罗森说道。", "links": [{"text": "Hulu", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/hulu/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这段合作孕育出了Hulu令人惊艳的新热播剧，该剧于7月27日首播，前三集一次性上线，随后在8月31日之前每周更新。《Furious》讲述了联邦调查局特工爱丽丝·布莱克（罗森饰）追捕连环杀手凯瑟琳（罗拉·佩蒂克鲁饰）的故事，后者的故事让加害者与受害者的界限变得扑朔迷离。其悬念不仅在于谁会被抓，还在于那些肩负保护人民职责的机构是否值得信赖来伸张正义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_A0847.jpg?w=650", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗森有一种天赋，能让复杂的女性角色变得饱满而生动，从充满活力的《安吉琳》到受伤却坚韧的爱丽丝。但在第1集的一个场景中，爱丽丝邀请一个男人进屋并与之搏斗，最初甚至让她想把剧本扔出房间。", "links": [{"text": "“Angelyne”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/shows/angelyne-review-emmy-rossum-peacock-1234722800/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "理解这个场景意味着要去体会一个既能充满力量、屡次遭受侵害，又会被危险所吸引以借此感到自己还活着的女性。爱丽丝与自我的隔绝也与她极其残酷的职业紧密相连，罗森表示，在这个职业中，“任何脆弱以及与自己内心的情感联系都不是资产，而是负债”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为这个复杂的世界寻找声音的工作也很早就开始了。马克斯曾与梅丽韦瑟合作过《Dying for Sex》，她在剧本阶段就加入了进来，在最终剪辑和死线到来缩小种种可能之前进行实验：“她能找到一种方法，让一切都显得无比真实，让你在不该笑的时候笑出来，并对一个你原本以为无法共情的人产生真正的同理心，”马克斯说。", "links": [{"text": "“Dying for Sex,”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/shows/dying-for-sex-review-michelle-williams-hulu-comedy-1235112174/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "原本更具爵士风的配乐逐渐被精简，其标志性元素演变为了“脆弱、低沉的女性嗓音”和工业打击乐。梅丽韦瑟鼓励马克斯在为那些本可能招致常规连环杀手套路的行为配乐时，要记住凯瑟琳完整的人性。“不，要记住她是谁的其他方面，”马克斯回忆起自己受到的提醒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B1175-032.jpg?w=650", "alt": "艾莉森·福尔曼出席在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶Vidiots举办的IndieWire x Hulu《Furious》展映活动，摄于2026年10月16日。", "caption": "艾莉森·福尔曼出席在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶Vidiots举办的IndieWire x Hulu《Furious》展映活动，摄于2026年10月16日。", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种对情感复杂性的关注也塑造了爱丽丝与由伯恩斯坦饰演的另一位特工诺拉·华盛顿之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“诺拉这个角色，在我看来，是有史以来写得最棒的角色之一，”伯恩斯坦说。尽管诺拉起初在某种程度上对爱丽丝进行了“军训式的捉弄”，但她慢慢地在这位年轻特工身上看到了自己的影子。演员们很容易就培养出了这种羁绊。“我觉得我们就像一家人，”伯恩斯坦说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就罗森而言，她表示在试戏前就知道伯恩斯坦是诺拉的不二人选，而之后的合作更是印证了这一点。她赞扬了搭档的勇敢、脆弱和对表演的投入：这些特质让她能够在悲剧色彩与喜剧效果之间游刃有余。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种坦荡令伯恩斯坦成为了其他杰出艺术家的首选合作对象，其中包括《沉默的羔羊》导演乔纳森·戴米。她回忆起这位已故电影人在他们合作《蕾切尔的婚礼》以及舞台剧《家庭周》时给予的巨大善意，并将后者的经历形容为“美好而又一团糟”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B0906-007.jpg?w=650", "alt": "埃米·罗森与昆西·泰勒·伯恩斯坦于 2026年10月16日 在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶 Vidiots 举行的 IndieWire x Hulu《Furious》放映活动上。", "caption": "埃米·罗森与昆西·泰勒·伯恩斯坦出席在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶Vidiots举办的IndieWire x Hulu《Furious》展映活动，摄于2026年10月16日。", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《Furious》剧组中，这种探索精神在罗森身上找到了热情的伙伴。她回忆起在片场看着伯恩斯坦演戏并对她说：“我已经迫不及待想让你看看你刚才演得有多好了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种喜爱也延伸到了韦身上，罗森高度赞扬了韦平衡幽默与真实情感的能力。由于剧中涉及人口贩运、性侵犯以及针对妇女和儿童的暴力等题材，她着重强调了掌控这种表演幅度有多么重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“据统计，这个房间里就会有人亲身经历过这些事情，”罗森说，“我认为拥有这些轻松的时刻至关重要，这样我们才能一起走进那些非常真实的情境中。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Seeking justice can be a lonely business. Making “Furious” was a team effort.

That distinction was warmly apparent when Emmy Rossum , Quincy Tyler Bernstine, Steve Way, and composer Ariel Marx gathered at Vidiots on October 16 for IndieWire and Disney’s “Pass the Remote” screening of Episode 1 and a conversation about bringing “ Furious ” to life.

With Halloween decorations filling the lobby and a deeply invested audience carrying the conversation into a reception afterward, the evening celebrated a cutting-edge thriller that finds connection in some very dark places. Way stole the show, much as he does in the buzzy crime series — despite his character, Alden, never appearing in the episode we screened. The actor teased that Alden’s encounters with law enforcement offered a chance to make the role personal.

“If I was in this situation,” he recalled thinking, “How would I… fuck with the feds?”

His answer plays out later in “Furious,” but the show’s blistering comic timing was on full display at Vidiots . Getting this particular group of troublemakers together began with Rossum embarking on a retro viewing project several summers back. Four years ago, the star and executive producer said she was hunting for older films with ideas worth developing into a long-form series.

That search led her to Bob Rafelson’s “Black Widow,” the 1987 thriller starring Debra Winger and Theresa Russell. She was fascinated by its evolution from an FBI agent’s pursuit of a female serial killer into an unusually moving relationship between two very different women.

“I just impregnated her with the idea of creating the show,” Rossum joked of creator Elizabeth Meriwether, taking care to credit the writer as the real “Furious” mastermind.

Rossum brought the project to Searchlight and Hulu , which had previously worked with Meriwether on “The Dropout.” Later, asked whether she liked the writer’s work, Rossum had an immediate answer. “It was a slam dunk yes for me,” Rossum said.

The partnership produced Hulu’s electric new hit, which premiered July 27 with three episodes before rolling out the rest weekly through August 31. “Furious” follows FBI agent Alice Black (Rossum) as she pursues Catherine (Lola Petticrew), a serial killer whose story complicates the distinction between perpetrator and victim. Its suspense extends beyond who will be caught to whether the institutions charged with protecting people can be trusted to deliver justice.

Rossum has a gift for making complicated women feel fully, vividly alive, from the effervescent “Angelyne” to the wounded, tenacious Alice. But a scene in Episode 1, in which Alice invites a man inside to fight him, initially made even her want to throw the script across the room.

Understanding it meant inhabiting a woman who could be powerful, repeatedly victimized, and drawn toward danger as a means of feeling alive. Alice’s disconnection from herself is also bound up in her particularly brutal profession, where, Rossum said, “any vulnerability and emotional connection to yourself is not an asset, it’s a liability.”

Finding the sound of that complicated world began early, too. Marx, who had collaborated with Meriwether on “Dying for Sex,” joined during the script stage, experimenting before finished cuts and deadlines narrowed the possibilities: “She finds a way to make everything feel incredibly authentic and to make you laugh when you don’t feel like you should and to really empathize for someone you didn’t think you could,” Marx said.

An initially jazzier score gradually became stripped down, its defining elements emerging as “vulnerable, guttural female voices” and industrial percussion. Meriwether encouraged Marx to remember Catherine’s full humanity when scoring behavior that might otherwise invite familiar serial-killer cues. “No, remember the other aspects of who she is,” Marx recalled being reminded.

That attention to emotional complexity also shaped Alice’s relationship with fellow agent Nora Washington, played by Bernstine.

“Nora, that character, in my opinion, is one of the greatest roles ever written,” Bernstine said. Although Nora initially “hazes” Alice to an extent, she slowly recognizes something of herself in the younger agent. Developing that bond came easily to the cast. “I feel like we’re family,” Bernstine said.

For her part, Rossum said she knew Bernstine was right for Nora before their chemistry read, and working together only confirmed it. She praised her co-star’s bravery, vulnerability, and willingness to play: qualities that let her move effortlessly between pathos and comedy.

That openness has made Bernstine a collaborator of choice for other remarkable artists, including “The Silence of the Lambs” director Jonathan Demme. She recalled the late filmmaker’s tremendous kindness during their work together on “Rachel Getting Married,” as well as the stage production “Family Week,” describing the latter experience as “beautiful and messy.”

On “Furious,” that spirit of discovery found an enthusiastic partner in Rossum, who remembered watching Bernstine onset and telling her, “I can’t wait for you to watch what you just did.”

The affection extended to Way, whose ability to balance humor and authentic emotion Rossum praised heavily. With material involving trafficking, sexual assault, and violence against women and children, she stressed just how much mastery over that range matters.

“Statistically there will be people in this room who have experienced these things firsthand,” Rossum said. “I think it’s incredibly important to have those moments of levity so that we can go to those very real places together.”

Way understood that responsibility through an especially personal lens. His healthcare writing often makes him angry, he explained, but comedy helps audiences receive his more challenging ideas with a sense of curiosity and grace. Alden’s relationship with the dangerous Catherine also allows “Furious” to serve as a different kind of recognition. Both characters know what it means to need help from systems that have failed them and seeking that support becomes a radical act.

Rossum described a parallel connection between F.B.I. agent Alice and Catherine, as well: “There’s almost like this non-sexual love story between them because they feel seen together,” she said.

Of course, there was plenty more to discuss; some requiring considerable spoiler restraint. About half the audience raised their hands before the screening to indicate they had already seen “Furious.” And afterward in the lobby, fans and guests struggled to keep late-season revelations to themselves. That’s an endorsement of bingeing the now-complete season if you haven’t seen it yet.

Beneath the laughter ran a celebration of disability in comedy, with Way’s command of the room demonstrating exactly why Alden shines in the show. Asked when he knew the series had accomplished something special, the actor described waking up to messages from disabled people he had never met, thanking him: “It’s heavy. It’s really heavy,” Way said.

Before “Furious,” the performer and comedian had gone three and a half years without doing a television show. But Meriwether wrote Alden just for Way: “She and I together have raised the bar for what it means to have authentic and accurate disability representation on TV,” he said.

For a team telling a story about broken systems, those messages offered a meaningful measure of success. With Season 2 already confirmed, there’s reason to hope television will keep making room for critical stories like these. “The fact that disabled people would go out of their way to say thank you,” Way said, “I think we did it.”

Watch the complete panel in the video above.

“Furious” Season 1 is now streaming on Hulu.

article_text:
Walter Koenig , who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the 1960s Star Trek TV series and several subsequent movies about the adventures of the USS Enterprise, died Sunday, according to his rep. He was 90.

Zachery McGinnis of Galactic Productions posted Monday on Facebook that Koenig died of natural causes in North Hollywood but did not provide other details.

Related Stories

2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries

‘Star Trek’s George Takei Pays Tribute To Walter Koenig: “My Heart Is Heavy”

“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen,” McGinnis wrote in part. “Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.”

George Takei, who played Sulu on the original Star Trek , also posted on Koenig’s death. See his and McGinnis’ posts below.

Koenig played the Russian navigator Chekov in second and third seasons of NBC’s Star Trek series from 1967-69 and reprised the role in the first seven Star Trek films from 1979-94. The character’s introduction for Season 2 came at the height of the U.S.-USSR Cold War.

The news comes as the original hugely popular, influential and low-budget Star Trek series created by Gene Roddenberry is marking its 60th anniversary . The show also was notable for its iconoclastic diversity for a mid-century TV series.

Born on September 14, 1936, in Chicago, Koenig had a brief early career as a dancer before turning to acting. His earliest roles including guest spots on such 1960s TV series as Combat!, The Untouchables, Ben Casey, Gidget, I Spy, The Alfred Hitchcock Hour and Jericho. He also appeared in the 1963 pilot episode of what would become one of TV’s most popular soap operas, ABC’s General Hospital.

But his big break would come with Star Trek in 1967 — the start of a 25-year journey as navigator of the starship USS Enterprise. The original series launched a universe that has kept tens of millions of Earthlings, known as Trekkies or Trekkers, enthralled for six decades.

“That camaraderie among Star Trek fans became more extensive when they started having conventions,” Koenig said in a 2013 interview for the TV Academy Foundation. “It wasn’t only what you’d traditionally call nerds. It was people who had a sense of humanity and a sense of justice. People who had imagination and people who loved monsters. It covered a much larger canvas than was initially thought.” Watch Koenig discuss his Star Trek origins and more — including how he hadn’t watched the show before his casting — in that interview here:

Star Trek was not widely popular during its initial 1960s run, never placing within the year-end Top 30 among primetime series during its three seasons in an era dominated by rural comedies, westerns and variety shows. Its peak audience was for the pre-Koenig first season in 1966-67, when it ranked No. 52 in the three-network universe. But it began a second life in syndication during the 1970s that made it among the most popular TV series — indeed, media properties — of all time.

Keonig appeared in three dozen episodes of Star Trek and continued to guest on such popular TV shows as Medical Center, The Virginian, Ironside and Columbo during the 1970s, also appearing in a handful of TV movies and the 1974 feature. But his career would go intergalactic again with the 1979 release of Star Trek: The Motion Picture, which reunited the original series’ cast. Wildly popular and drenched in high-tech special effects, the film had a then-record domestic opening of nearly $12 million and ranked among the year-end Top 5.

Its success fueled five numbered sequels starring the original cast in 1982, 1984, 1986, 1989 and 1991 — all of which featured Koenig as Chekov. He also appeared in the transitional 1994 feature Star Trek: Generations, which introduced Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) as the new captain of the Enterprise, along with several other new characters who would star in more Star Trek projects.

Koenig’s death leaves Takei and William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk, as the lone surviving main cast members of the original Star Trek series.

RELATED: James Doohan, Who Played Scotty On ‘Star Trek’, Had Ashes Taken To International Space Station

Koenig’s TV and film castmate Takei, who played Lt. Hikaru Sulu, paid tribute to him on Monday, writing:

“My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today. “Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. “Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.

While Koenig voiced Chekov in several Trek -related video games, podcasts and other media, he also enjoyed a long screen career outside the Star Trek universe, notably recurring as the villainous Psi Corps senior officer Alfred Bester in a dozen episodes of the syndicated space drama Babylon 5 from 1994-98.

His guest-starring TV roles during the past few decades included Diagnosis Murder, Son of a Beach, Renegades and playing himself on the animated Futurama and voicing multiple characters in several episodes of Netflix’s toon series Stretch Armstrong and the Flex Fighters . Koenig also appeared in several movies along with numerous documentaries, talk shows, awards shows and others.

Information on survivors and a memorial service was incomplete.

Here is McGinnis’ full post on Koenigs death:

Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece. Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in Star Trek: The Original Series, Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond Star Trek, his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film Mr. Fleischmann, for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards—a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft. Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it. On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades. Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before. Rest in peace.
